subtype: Approach: linking the chore to something he does anyway [Thinking]
passage: I'm Pallavi, and my little brother Chinmay used to dump his shoes and bag wherever he stood. Amma nagged, and it never worked. Then one day I saw him standing in the hallway, talking to himself. "When I come in and change my clothes, that's the moment. Shoes on the rack, bag on the hook. Same time, same place. Then I won't need to remember." He did it the next day, and the next. Now, when he comes in and pulls off his school shirt, I see him walk straight to the rack. Amma has stopped nagging, and honestly, I have too.

qa.q: Where does Chinmay put his bag?
qa.a: Chinmay puts his bag on the hook.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel about tying the job to changing his clothes?
qa.a: Chinmay feels confident it will work, because changing clothes happens anyway, so he says he won't need to remember the shoes and bag separately.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Chinmay try, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could put a picture note above the rack or ask a parent to remind him at first. Either could help until the habit is strong.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see the change in Chinmay?
qa.a: Pallavi watches the routine take hold and notes that Amma has stopped nagging, and admits to stopping too, so Pallavi seems relieved and a little impressed.

grounding: A boy links putting shoes on the rack and the bag on the hook to changing clothes after school, so he forgets less, as seen by a sibling.

subtype: Approach: linking the chore to something he does anyway [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Anand came home, kicked his shoes under the sofa and dropped his school bag by the door. Payal, his older sister, tripped over it and groaned. "Every single day, Anand."
Wednesday: Pulling on his home shorts, Anand stopped halfway. "I always change the minute I walk in," he thought. "I never forget that part. So what if the shoes go on the rack right after I change? Then the bag goes on the hook. Same order every time, no remembering needed."
The next Monday: He had missed the bag only once all week. Payal came into the hall, looked at the empty floor and raised her eyebrows. "Who cleaned up?"

qa.q: What does Anand say he never forgets to do when he walks in?
qa.a: He says he always changes the minute he walks in and never forgets that part.

qa.q: What does Anand's thinking on Wednesday suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He sounds hopeful and a little pleased with himself, because he has found a habit he never misses and can hang the new jobs onto it.

qa.q: What else could Anand try if the chain slips on a busy day, and why?
qa.a: He could stick a small drawing of shoes and a bag on the inside of the door, because a reminder at the exact spot catches the days when the habit alone fails.

qa.q: How does the new routine look to Payal?
qa.a: Payal is surprised to find the hall clear, and probably relieved that she no longer trips over his bag every evening.

grounding: It shows a boy attaching two small tidying jobs to the change of clothes he does every day so that he forgets them less.

subtype: Approach: linking the chore to something he does anyway [Thinking]
passage: Swati, beti, your sandals are in the kitchen again. Sit, let your Dada Nilesh tell you something. When I was a boy in Nashik, I lost one chappal every week. My mother scolded me each evening, and I felt small, because I did want to be good. One day I noticed something. Every evening, the first thing I did was wash my feet at the tap by the door; Amma would not let anyone in otherwise, so I never skipped it. I thought, the tap is my bell. Feet washed, then chappals under the bench, then satchel on the nail. Tap, bench, nail. I said it in my head for a week. After a month my hands did it without me. Amma stopped scolding. Now, beti, what do you always do when you come in?

qa.q: Where did young Nilesh wash his feet every evening?
qa.a: Young Nilesh washed his feet at the tap by the door.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel when his mother scolded him about the lost chappals?
qa.a: Young Nilesh felt small and a bit ashamed, because Nilesh did want to be good but kept forgetting.

qa.q: What other approach could young Nilesh have tried if the tap trick had not worked?
qa.a: Young Nilesh could have asked Amma to remind him for the first few days, or kept a basket right beside the tap, so the job was impossible to walk past.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's Amma have seen the change in him?
qa.a: Amma would have been pleased and surprised to find the chappals under the bench every evening, with no need to scold.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a boy, he tied putting away his chappals and satchel to a daily habit and stopped forgetting.
